> **[case-study]**
> **Recruitment Process (RP)**
> 
> RP is a private limited company based in country Z. RP is an employment agency that operates in a dynamic business environment. To survive in the market RP must be efficient and maintain a good reputation. RP uses social media to attract customers and relies on word-of-mouth recommendations. RP has recently won an award for its diversity and equality practices.
> 
> RP's customers provide details of the roles and number of employees required. RP quotes a price to its customer and then agrees a contract to provide its services at the price quoted.
> 
> Ray, Managing Director, has asked Adjil, Finance Director, to provide a budget breakdown of a recent customer contract. RP's staff are specialist recruiters who find the appropriate employees for each job role.
> 
> **Table 1.1 RP's budget for a recent customer contract, March 2024**
> 
> | Job role | Number of employees required | Specialist recruiters required | Cost per specialist recruiter (\$000) | Total cost (\$000) |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | Warehouse | 70 | 1 | 100 | 100 |
> | Sales | 225 | 3 | 120 | 360 |
> | Technology | 145 | 3 | 140 | 420 |
> | Management | 10 | 2 | 190 | 380 |
> | **Total** | **450** |   |   | **1260** |
> 
> Adjil noted that the actual cost per employee recruited showed an adverse variance of \$500.
> 
> Ray is concerned that the budget does not accurately show the costs to RP. Ray thinks this is because of inefficient practices in the recruitment process.

Explain the term *employment agency*.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> | Marks | Knowledge & Application |
> |---|---|
> | **3** | Knowledge of employment agency + explanation + applied to a business context |
> | **2** | Knowledge + explanation, OR knowledge + applied to a business context |
> | **1** | Knowledge of employment agency only |
> | **0** | No creditable response |
> 
> **Indicative content** — *AO1 Knowledge and understanding*
> 
> - Provides recruitment services to other businesses
> - A business outsources recruitment of employees to another business
> - Finds ideal candidates for a specific job role
> 
> **AO2 Application** — *explanation of employment agency*
> 
> - Customer provides details of job roles and numbers required — the agency selects and recruits employees
> - Specialist recruiters used — providing expertise which may not exist in a business
> - Increased efficiency / lower cost — especially where many and varied roles / employees are required
> - Can provide training / manuals — reducing costs for other businesses
> 
> **Application to a business context** (RP or any other scenario)
> 
> - Example of a business using an employment agency, e.g. a retailer outsourcing seasonal hiring to an agency like RP
> 
> Accept all valid responses

> **[exam-tip]**
> Three marks split K + EXP + CTX. Key idea: an employment agency is HIRED BY another business to find candidates on its behalf. Apply to RP via the table — 'RP's customer specified 450 employees across four roles; RP supplied specialist recruiters to source them'. Don't confuse with a job centre (which is open to anyone seeking work).

Analyse **two** methods RP could use to select sales employees.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> | Level | AO1 Knowledge and understanding (2 marks) | AO2 Application (2 marks) | AO3 Analysis (4 marks) |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **2** |   |   | **3–4 marks — Developed analysis**: developed analysis identifying connections between causes, impacts and / or consequences of **two** points (4) or **one** point (3) |
> | **1** | **1–2 marks**: knowledge of **two** relevant methods (2) or **one** relevant method (1) | **1–2 marks**: application of **two** relevant points (2) or **one** relevant point (1) to RP | **1–2 marks — Limited analysis**: limited analysis of **two** points (2) or **one** point (1) |
> | **0** | No creditable response | No creditable response | No creditable response |
> 
> **Note: must be SELECTION methods, not recruitment.**
> 
> **Indicative content** — *AO1 Knowledge and understanding* (max 2 marks: 1 per method)
> 
> Selection methods include:
> 
> - Curriculum vitae (CV) / résumé
> - Application forms
> - Interview
> - References
> - Testing
> - Assessment centres
> 
> **AO2 Application** — *context applied to selecting sales employees* (max 1 mark per method)
> 
> - Sales role requires customer contact and selling skills — assessment centre useful
> - 225 sales employees required but only 3 specialist recruiters — simple, quick method best (application form + references)
> - Sales staff must be personable — interview to check character / fit
> - Already showing adverse variance — costly methods reduce profit further
> - Use of Table 1.1
> 
> **AO3 Analysis** (4 marks total: 2 per method)
> 
> *Method 1 example* — 'application form + references'
> 
> - *Developed (2): with 225 sales hires needed and only 3 recruiters, application forms allow fast screening at scale; references verify track record without the cost of individual interviews — keeps cost per hire close to the \$2800 budget*
> 
> *Method 2 example* — 'short interview'
> 
> - *Developed (2): sales staff need personality and customer-facing skills that paper applications can't reveal; a brief interview confirms fit, reducing the risk of bad hires that would push the adverse variance higher*
> 
> Other angles:
> 
> - High cost of selection — lower profits / pushes adverse variance further
> - Many applicants — need quick / efficient method
> - Time scale of hiring — may not have time to interview all
> - Need to ensure equality and diversity in selection — RP has won an award for this
> 
> Accept all valid responses

> **[exam-tip]**
> The 4 analysis marks split 2 + 2 across two methods. The scale challenge is the key: 225 sales hires with only 3 recruiters drives selection design. Pick CONTRASTING methods — e.g. application form (fast, paper-based, scalable) and short interview (slower, but verifies personality). Don't pick two methods that test the same thing. Watch the question: SELECTION (after recruitment, choosing between candidates), not RECRUITMENT (attracting candidates).

Evaluate the impact on RP of diversity and equality in the workplace.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> | Level | AO1 Knowledge and understanding (2 marks) | AO2 Application (2 marks) | AO3 Analysis (2 marks) | AO4 Evaluation (6 marks) |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | **3** |   |   |   | **5–6 marks — Developed evaluation in context**: developed judgement / conclusion in RP context; developed evaluative comments which balance some key arguments in context |
> | **2** | **2 marks**: developed knowledge of relevant key term(s) / factor(s) | **2 marks**: developed application of relevant point(s) to RP | **2 marks**: developed analysis identifying connections between causes, impacts and / or consequences | **3–4 marks — Developed evaluation**: developed judgement / conclusion; developed evaluative comments which balance some key arguments |
> | **1** | **1 mark**: limited knowledge | **1 mark**: limited application | **1 mark**: limited analysis | **1–2 marks — Limited evaluation**: judgement with limited supporting evidence; an attempt to balance the arguments |
> | **0** | No creditable response | No creditable response | No creditable response | No creditable response |
> 
> **Indicative content** — *AO1 Knowledge and understanding* (max 2 marks)
> 
> *Diversity and equality:*
> 
> - **Equality** — ensuring a fair organisation so everyone has the opportunity to fulfil their potential
> - **Diversity** — creating a mixed workforce, placing a positive value on diversity in the workplace
> 
> *Impacts of diversity and equality:*
> 
> - May be required by legislation
> - Good employer reputation
> - Easier to attract new employees
> - May get the best applicants
> - Introduces new ideas / innovation
> 
> **AO2 Application** — *context applied to RP* (max 2 marks)
> 
> - Outsourcing company so other businesses likely require a diverse work organisation — better fit with customers
> - Businesses more likely to use RP if it has good equality practices
> - Adverse variance of \$500 per hire — indicates need to ensure efficiency
> - Dynamic market environment requires creative employees
> - Uses social media to attract customers — variety of languages helps global expansion
> - Won an award for good equality and diversity practices
> - Use of Table 1.1
> 
> **AO3 Analysis** (max 2 marks)
> 
> - Change of working culture may be required — increasing costs / unsettled environment
> - Training in equality and diversity for existing employees — higher costs / lower profit
> - Costs of recruiting with additional requirements — higher costs
> - Diverse ways of working and thinking — bring in new ideas — increase competitiveness
> - Increase productivity — employees motivated by good working practices — increased profit
> - Better able to operate in a global marketplace — attract more customers / businesses — increased sales / revenue
> 
> **AO4 Evaluation** (6 marks)
> 
> A judgement about the impact on RP of diversity and equality in the workplace. Possible evaluative points:
> 
> - Weighing up risks vs. reward of diversity
> - Short-term costs vs. long-term benefits
> - Judgement of consequences to RP and impact on stakeholders
> - Challenges posed to company culture
> 
> **Evaluation mark band guidance**
> 
> - **Eval 6** — developed judgement / conclusion in RP context **[6 marks]**
> - **Eval 5** — developed evaluative comments in RP context **[5 marks]**
> - **Eval 4** — developed judgement without context **[4 marks]**
> - **Eval 3** — developed evaluative comments without context **[3 marks]**
> - **Eval 2** — judgement with little supporting evidence **[2 marks]**
> - **Eval 1** — an attempt to balance arguments **[1 mark]**
> 
> Accept all valid responses

> **[exam-tip]**
> The pivot: RP HAS WON AN AWARD for its diversity / equality practices — so the impact is partly already realised (reputation, employer-of-choice for diverse talent). Argue benefits (customer fit for diverse hiring needs, attracts top talent, dynamic environment needs varied perspectives) but balance against costs (training, recruitment process complexity, possible adverse variance). Anchor your judgement on RP being an EMPLOYMENT AGENCY (its diversity reputation directly affects whether clients hire them).

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Cobblestone Shoes (CS)**
> 
> Yazeem is a highly skilled shoemaker. He opened CS in 1975, as a sole trader, to design and repair shoes. When Yazeem set up CS the main target market was professional people who wanted shoes to wear to work or to dress smartly. He produced the shoes using batch production and sold them in his own shop. Each design of shoe was made in a range of sizes and colours.
> 
> Recently there has been an increase in low-priced shoes produced for the mass market, which has reduced Yazeem's sales of new shoes. It has also reduced the demand for shoe repairs.
> 
> Yazeem's daughter, Abir, is keen to take over the running of CS. She has been fully trained in making shoes and feels that it is time for Yazeem to retire.
> 
> Abir thinks that the business should be targeting niche markets. She would like to design and produce unique shoes and use price skimming to increase the profitability of the business.
> 
> Abir is also concerned about the contribution made on each batch of shoes. Table 2.1 shows some break-even data for a recent batch of shoes.
> 
> **Table 2.1 Break-even data about a recent batch of shoes**
> 
> | Item | Value |
> |---|---|
> | Break-even level of output | 400 units |
> | Margin of safety | 100 units |
> | Total variable costs | \$18 750 |
> | Total costs | \$23 750 |
> | Total revenue | \$25 000 |
> 
> Abir has suggested that CS should adopt a just in time (JIT) approach to inventory management. By using JIT, she argues, CS would be able to increase its working capital and avoid having money tied up in inventory that might not be used or sold. CS currently has a large number of shoes on display in the shop. There is also a large amount of their main raw material, which is leather and must be kept in a climate-controlled storage area.
> 
> Abir has already found a new local supplier which is happy to deliver inventory as required.

Identify **one** type of training.

> - On-the-job
> - Off-the-job

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Post Scent (PS)**
> 
> PS is a private limited company operating in country H. It sells perfume for men and women using its own website. PS purchases the perfume in large quantities from various manufacturers and then sells it in smaller quantities to its customers. Most of the perfumes are sold in glass bottles.
> 
> PS has two main ways in which it sells perfume:
> 
> - A website where customers can purchase a range of perfumes. The perfumes are priced to be lower than high street competitors.
> - A subscription service where customers pay a monthly fee for a mystery perfume to be delivered each month.
> 
> All of PS's products are delivered to customers' homes using the postal service. The packages can be left in a mailbox or in a safe place outside of the home. PS has an aim to improve the sustainability of its operations.
> 
> PS uses incremental budgeting. Table 1.1 shows the budgeted and actual cost and revenue data for 2023.
> 
> **Table 1.1 Budgeted and actual cost and revenue data for 2023 (\$000)**
> 
> | Item | Budgeted | Actual | Variance |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Revenue | 500 | 600 | **x** |
> | Direct costs | 300 | 350 | **y** |
> | Indirect costs | 150 | 125 | **z** |
> 
> The directors of PS have decided that the business needs a Marketing Manager. The role of the Marketing Manager will be:
> 
> - to plan the recruitment and training of a new sales team
> - to organise the production of digital promotions
> - to advise the Board of Directors on changes to the PS product portfolio.
> 
> The directors have shortlisted five suitable applicants and plan to invite them all to an assessment centre as part of the recruitment process.

Analyse **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage to PS of using an assessment centre when selecting a Marketing Manager.
parts.solution_md:
**Mark Scheme and Guidance** (two-sided: max 4 marks per side)

| Level | AO1 Knowledge and understanding (2 marks: max 1 per side) | AO2 Application (2 marks: max 1 per side) | AO3 Analysis (4 marks: max 2 per side) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **2** |   |   | **3–4 marks — Developed analysis**: developed analysis identifying connections between causes, impacts and / or consequences of **two** points (4) or **one** point (3) |
| **1** | **1–2 marks**: knowledge of **two** relevant points (2) or **one** relevant point (1) | **1–2 marks**: application of **two** relevant points (2) or **one** relevant point (1) to PS | **1–2 marks — Limited analysis**: limited analysis of **two** points (2) or **one** point (1) |
| **0** | No creditable response | No creditable response | No creditable response |

*Max 1 knowledge mark if no advantage / disadvantage of an assessment centre is identified.*

**Indicative content** — *AO1 Knowledge and understanding*

*Knowledge of an assessment centre:*

- A combination of tasks and activities that test suitability for the job
- Chance to demonstrate a wider range of skills than during a traditional face-to-face interview
- Hosted over anything from an afternoon to two days
- Often the final stage of the selection process
- A group of candidates usually attend together

*Advantages:*

- More suitable / knowledgeable / skilled recruit
- Wider skilled recruit / more skills tested
- More detailed process
- Useful as final stage of recruitment
- Allows direct comparison with other candidates

*Disadvantages:*

- Takes more time
- Cost of an assessment centre
- Not realistic / not linked to specific employment / may assess unnecessary skills / knowledge

**AO2 Application** — *context applied to PS*

- Marketing Manager role: plan recruitment / training of new sales team, organise digital promotions, advise Board on product portfolio
- Tasks relating to marketing of PS (perfume, website sales, subscription sales, packaging)
- Five shortlisted applicants
- Use of Table 1.1 (PS profit / variance position)

**AO3 Analysis** (max 2 marks per side)

*Advantages:*

- More suitable recruit — better marketing decisions — lower costs of marketing — increase profitability
- Wider skilled recruit — better digital promotions — higher sales — increase profits
- Longer process than an interview — more likely to find a better candidate — increase sales and growth of PS
- Final stage of recruitment — suitable way to distinguish between qualified and similar candidates — increase chances of getting the best candidate
- Allows direct comparison — increases probability of finding the best candidate to improve PS's marketing

*Disadvantages:*

- Takes more time — increase costs — reduces profitability
- May assess unnecessary skills, provides an unrealistic image — increases probability of choosing the wrong candidate — long-run cost (more recruitment needed)
- Cost of an assessment centre — significantly more expensive than an interview, especially for all five shortlisted applicants — decreased profitability

Accept all valid responses

**End of Mark Scheme and Guidance**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a TWO-SIDED 8-marker: 4 marks for the advantage, 4 marks for the disadvantage. Each side splits as 1K + 1APP + 2AN. Pick CONTRASTING points — e.g. ADV: 'better-quality hire = better digital promotions = higher sales'; DIS: 'cost of running the centre for all five applicants reduces short-term profit'. Don't pick two advantages or two disadvantages by accident.

parts.problem_md: Evaluate whether cooperation between management and the workforce is the most important factor in the success of a car manufacturer.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> | Level | AO1 Knowledge and understanding (2 marks) | AO2 Application (2 marks) | AO3 Analysis (2 marks) | AO4 Evaluation (6 marks) |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | **3** |   |   |   | **5–6 marks — Developed evaluation in context**: developed judgement / conclusion in the business context; developed evaluative comments which balance some key arguments in context |
> | **2** | **2 marks**: developed knowledge of relevant key term(s) / factor(s) | **2 marks**: developed application of relevant point(s) to the business context | **2 marks**: developed analysis identifying connections between causes, impacts and / or consequences | **3–4 marks — Developed evaluation**: developed judgement / conclusion; developed evaluative comments which balance some key arguments |
> | **1** | **1 mark**: limited knowledge | **1 mark**: limited application | **1 mark**: limited analysis | **1–2 marks — Limited evaluation**: judgement with limited supporting evidence; an attempt is made to balance the arguments |
> | **0** | No creditable response | No creditable response | No creditable response | No creditable response |
> 
> **Indicative content** — *AO1 Knowledge and understanding*
> 
> - Cooperation is the action or process of working together to achieve the same goal
> - A state of relations where employee and management work together to accomplish certain goals using mutually acceptable means
> - It is the outcome of a continuous process of enhancing mutual trust and respecting through sharing information, discussion, consultation and negotiation
> - Success can be defined by many factors: market share, profits, share value, productivity, labour turnover, employee relations, environmental credentials, brand image
> 
> **AO2 Application** (car manufacturer)
> 
> - Need to cooperate in different teams that work on different parts of the car such as chassis
> - Companies like Nissan have Kaizen that involves cooperation between management and workers
> - Car manufacturer related terms, e.g. tyres, chassis, robots, assembly, quality circles, quality assurance, production targets, safety, car designs, TQM
> - Named businesses, e.g. Ford, BMW, Skoda, Audi, Nissan
> 
> **AO3 Analysis**
> 
> - Cooperation can lead to a more harmonious workplace — improve productivity — reduce labour turnover
> - A strong ethos of cooperation and teamwork — where ideas are shared — means objectives and goals can be achieved successfully — customers are satisfied
> - A sense that everyone is pulling in the same direction — invested in business success — can increase productivity — morale — attract the best workers
> - Training and resources may be required to ensure effective cooperation — which can increase costs
> - Goals that ensure different teams cooperate — can improve productivity and morale
> - Communication channels between all related parties, including unions, need to work — ensure harmonious industrial relations
> - Employees need to be empowered to contribute — creative ideas could give the business a competitive edge — or help streamline production
> - Less employee conflict — managers can focus on helping the team achieve objectives — more cars made in shorter period
> - Mutual respect between managers and workers — willingness to perform well — goals achieved
> - Cooperation enables a trusting environment — employees take risks — better engagement — improve retention
> - Workers may need to feel valued financially first — if not, industrial action — production stops
> 
> **AO4 Evaluation**
> 
> A judgement / conclusion is made that cooperation between managers and the workforce is the most important factor in the success of a car manufacturer. Possible evaluative points:
> 
> - A conclusion that cooperation is just one factor in success — marketing or product quality may be equally important
> - A judgement that other business activities are more important, such as marketing strategies — they need to make the right car or it won't sell
> - A conclusion about what the car manufacturer hopes to achieve in the long and short term and whether this is dependent on cooperation
> - A judgement that the onus lies on good leadership to make cooperation work, or that it depends on employee motivations — not everyone wants to cooperate
> - A judgement that cooperation may depend on how well represented workers are by a union
> - A judgement that enhanced productivity is key to a successful car manufacturer — should be achieved by any means necessary
> - A judgement that car manufacturers operate in an internationally competitive market — essential to do everything possible to foster cooperation
> - A judgement about the environment in which the car manufacturer exists — subject to factors beyond its control (economic downturn, pandemic) — job security cannot be guaranteed
> - A judgement about cooperation depending on strength / role of trade unions, location factors, or how successfully the business changes to electric car production in comparison to competitors
> 
> **Evaluation mark band guidance**
> 
> - **Eval 6** — developed judgement / conclusion made in context (car manufacturer) **[6 marks]**
> - **Eval 5** — developed evaluative comments given in context **[5 marks]**
> - **Eval 4** — developed judgement / conclusion made, not in context **[4 marks]**
> - **Eval 3** — developed evaluative comments, not in context **[3 marks]**
> - **Eval 2** — judgement / conclusion with little supporting evidence, not in context **[2 marks]**
> - **Eval 1** — an attempt is made to balance arguments **[1 mark]**
> - **Eval 0** — no evaluation
> 
> Accept all valid responses

> **[exam-tip]**
> Car manufacturing is highly capital-intensive, unionised, and operates in a globally competitive market. Argue cooperation matters (Toyota's Kaizen, Nissan's lean production) but balance against equally important factors — product design, marketing, supply chain, EV transition, brand reputation. The top 6 marks need a judgement that names a specific car maker (Toyota, BMW, Ford) or a car-industry challenge (electric shift, union strikes).

> - Less employee training required
> - Staff loyalty and morale likely to be high
> - Less risk of work building up with gaps when staff leave
> - Consistency of production
> - Production quality maintained
> - Customer contact retained
> - Reputation of business high
>

> 
> - Less people leave the business, low replacement costs
> - Fewer employees require induction or other training
> - Staff content to stay in business
> - Sufficient numbers of staff maintained
> - Experienced workers remain in the business
> - Product quality maintained
> - Customers relate to known staff
> 
> **AO3 Analysis**
> 
> - Lower recruitment and training costs — means more money to reinvest in other areas of the business
> - Consistent customer relationships — means less chance of losing customers — maintain or even increase sales
> - Consistent quality of products and services — less errors — less waste / complaints — decreased costs / improved image
> - Low turnover might make business attractive when business does need to recruit — attract better quality workers
> - Better morale and team spirit — can lead to higher productivity

>

>

>

> - Work-life balance is about creating and maintaining supportive and healthy work environments that enable employees to have balance between work and other aspects of life — family, friends, community, personal growth
> - Employee welfare is overseen by HRM departments who may offer counselling and other services to staff in need of support, perhaps because of family or financial problems
> - HRM is the strategic approach to the effective management of an organisation's workers so that they help the business gain a competitive advantage
> 
> **AO2 Application** (local bus service)
> 
> - Bus drivers and conductors have stressful jobs
> - Bus drivers are required to drive safely
> - They need to be alert and not over-tired
> - Bus drivers and conductors are close to passengers
> - They need to work regularly to guarantee a bus timetable
> 
> **AO3 Analysis**
> 
> - WLB could lead to bus drivers feeling more optimistic about responsibilities — better able to meet timetable targets
> - Potentially lower labour turnover and absenteeism reduced if staff feel they have a good WLB
> - Bus drivers might have more energy and be less tired with good WLB — leading to better customer experience
> - Stressed and overworked bus staff may be rude or not deal very well with angry passengers — which might lead to customer complaints and demotivated / demoralised drivers
> - WLB could reduce negative effects of work-life conflict — such as health risks (smoking, drinking, weight gain, depression) on employees — business will build good image as a caring employer — leading to healthier drivers
> - Strengthen employee loyalty and productivity — which means buses might run on time — increase reputation and esteem for drivers
> - Duty of care to employees — means it will reduce likelihood of paying compensation to employees / customers if accidents occur to elderly passengers due to speeding drivers
> 
> **AO4 Evaluation**
> 
> A judgement / decision as to whether WLB is the most important HRM factor for employee welfare in a local bus service. Possible evaluative points:
> 
> - A judgement is made as to the importance of HR concern for WLB for the welfare of those working for a local bus service
> - How might WLB be an important HRM factor for employee welfare? — improve performance, improve morale of staff, prevent over-tiredness, signal concern for and confidence in staff
> - Might other HRM factors be equally / more important than WLB for the welfare of bus service staff, such as training, shorter work hours, more pay, better quality management / supervision, better canteen facilities, better holiday entitlements?
> 
> **Evaluation mark band guidance**
> 
> - **Eval 6** — developed judgement / conclusion made in context (local bus service) **[6 marks]**
> - **Eval 5** — developed evaluative comments given in context **[5 marks]**
> - **Eval 4** — developed judgement / conclusion made, not in context **[4 marks]**
> - **Eval 3** — developed evaluative comments, not in context **[3 marks]**
> - **Eval 2** — judgement / conclusion with little supporting evidence, not in context **[2 marks]**
> - **Eval 1** — an attempt is made to balance arguments **[1 mark]**
> - **Eval 0** — no evaluation
> 
> Accept all valid responses

> **[exam-tip]**
> The 'local bus service' context is critical — driver fatigue directly threatens passenger safety, so WLB has a duty-of-care dimension other industries don't. Argue WLB matters (reduces accidents, lowers absenteeism, retains experienced drivers) but balance against equally important HRM factors (pay, training, supervision). parts.problem_md:
‘Human Resource Management is the most important department in any large manufacturing business.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Level 5 (17-20 marks)**
> 
> Effective evaluation of the view that Human Resource management is the most important department in any large manufacturing business.
> 
> Possible answers could include:
> 
> - HRM recruits and trains employees for all departments. Marketing, Finance, Operations, etc.
> - Without the most appropriate employees in each department the business is less likely to be successful.
> - A manufacturing business produces goods to sell to customers.
> - A manufacturing business needs to be able to obtain components and materials at the right quality and at the right price and time, therefore the Purchasing department is important.
> - The skills of the employees will impact on the productivity levels and the quality of the finished goods. HRM dept has to recruit and/or provide appropriate training for the employees involved in the manufacturing process.
> - HRM dept also keeps records of all personnel issues – helps succession planning and recognising training/promotion opportunities. Manufacturing can be highly technological and therefore it would be vital that employees update their skills from time to time.
> - The context is manufacturing therefore candidates will need to inject some context e.g. the design and quality of the finished product to the business; some reference to production etc. and how HRM dept impacts on that.
> - HRM department does not produce the finished product to supply to customers so might be considered of less importance.
> - HRM is only one of many functions in any business where strong interrelationships between all departments is generally through to be very important.
> - The evaluation could argue that HRM department is the most important due to its role in recruiting the best people for the job in all other departments.

parts.problem_md:
‘The most important role of human resource management (HRM) in a fast food restaurant is to maintain a high level of employee morale and welfare.’

Evaluate this view.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> AO1 out of 2 marks. 
> AO2 out of 2 marks. 
> AO3 out of 2 marks. 
> AO4 out of 6 marks.
> 
> **Indicative content **
> 
> Responses may include:
> 
> **AO1 Knowledge and understanding **
> 
> - HRM function is to plan, recruit and develop the workforce in order to achieve business objectives.
> - HRM includes a wide range of activities such as recruitment, training, motivation, contracts of employment, morale and welfare.
> - The emphasis in recent times is on morale and welfare, safety, working conditions and job satisfaction of employees.
> - Morale includes the emotions, attitudes and overall outlook of employees; welfare is anything that makes the workplace more congenial and healthy.
> 
> **AO2 Application **
> 
> - Morale and welfare increasingly seen as a vital part of HRM responsibility and particularly important to a service business like a fast food restaurant.
> - Quicker and more efficient customer service from employees who consider their morale and welfare is being supported.
> - Traditionally fast food industry has high level of turnover and often low job satisfaction.
> 
> **AO3 Analysis **
> 
> - Increasing morale and welfare is an important HRM function as it can increase job satisfaction, labour productivity and reduce labour turnover.
> - HRM contributes to employee morale and welfare when it efficiently and effectively carries out any responsibility in respect of the workforce – by, for example, administering an equitable remuneration system or providing appropriate training courses.
> - HRM is responsible for workforce planning and if this is poorly done then business efficiency will decline – e.g. too many or too few employees.
> - HRM is responsible for recruitment and selection of employees and this is important as employees need to be suited to the work.
> - HRM might well provide support and advice for staff with personal problems such as achieving a more sensible work-life balance.
> - HRM might ensure that policies on equality and diversity are fit for purpose.
> - HRM may see employee morale and welfare as a primary concern for an outward facing business such as a fast food restaurant.
> 
> **AO4 Evaluation **
> 
> - The importance of the involvement of HRM in issues relating to employee morale and welfare may well depend on the type of business and the maturity of that business.
> - There may be more pressing short-term problems facing HRM that might be more important such as skills shortages or industrial relations challenges.
> - The resolution of such problems will likely assist in improving general morale and welfare issues.
> - Suggestions may be made that some of the more specific responsibilities of HRM are more important than the pursuit of such nebulous concepts as employee morale and welfare.
> - Keeping costs low might be more important than employee morale and welfare.
> - In fast food restaurants building teamwork is important but there is also a need to follow rigid production processes.
> - Judgement made on whether maintaining morale and welfare of employees is the most important role of HRM.
> 
> Accept all valid responses.
